live_plab_copy.stem: Before taking a blood sample, which is the most important first safety step?

options.A: Check the patient's name against the bed board above the bed space
options.B: Ask the patient 'Are you John Smith?' and check the request form
options.C: Label the tubes in advance at the nurses' station to save time
options.D: Confirm identity from the bed number written on the request form
options.E: Confirm the patient's identity using appropriate identifiers

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Confirm the patient's identity using appropriate identifiers
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Positive patient identification, asking the patient to state their full name and date of birth and checking against the wristband/request form, is the essential first step, because wrong-blood-in-tube errors can lead to misdiagnosis and fatal transfusion reactions (SHOT; BSH guidance).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Bed boards are unreliable identifiers and do not confirm identity. B. Closed questions allow a patient to agree to the wrong name; patients should state their full name and date of birth. C. Labelling away from the patient is a major cause of wrong-blood-in-tube errors. D. Bed numbers are unreliable identifiers because patients move beds.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Positive patient identification means asking the patient to state their full name and date of birth and checking these against the wristband and request form; wrong-blood-in-tube errors can cause fatal transfusion reactions.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Correct patient identification is fundamental to safe blood sampling.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, asking 'Are you John Smith?' — it seems to involve the patient, but a closed question allows a confused or anxious patient to agree to the wrong name.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Identify the patient positively with open questions and the wristband before every sample.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient receives a prescription but says they cannot read the label because of severe visual impairment.

What should the healthcare professional do?

options.A: Ask a family member to manage the medicines instead
options.B: Provide the instructions in an accessible format
options.C: Switch to a once-daily medicine so no label is needed
options.D: Defer prescribing until a carer can attend
options.E: Give a printed leaflet with the standard instructions

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Provide the instructions in an accessible format
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Patients should be given information in a form they can access and understand so that treatment can be used safely.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Responsibility should not be shifted to relatives without the patient's agreement. C. Changing treatment does not address the need for accessible information. D. Treatment should not be delayed because of a disability. E. Standard print is not accessible to someone who cannot read the label.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Reasonable adjustments, such as large-print or braille labels, verbal explanation or audio information, let patients with sight loss take their medicines safely and independently.
live_plab_copy.thinking: New prescription ↓ Severe visual impairment ↓ Cannot read standard label ↓ Duty to make reasonable adjustments ↓ Provide information in an accessible format
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, ask a family member to manage the medicines — it seems practical, but it removes the patient's independence without their agreement; adapt the format instead.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Adapt the format of information to the patient; do not hand their care to others.

live_plab_copy.stem:
An older adult appears frightened when their relative enters the room. They privately disclose that the relative has been taking their money.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Discuss the allegation with the relative in front of the patient
options.B: Advise the patient to contact their bank and take no further action
options.C: Document the disclosure but take no action as it is not medical
options.D: Take it seriously, assess safety and follow safeguarding procedures
options.E: Tell the patient financial matters are outside the clinical role

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Take it seriously, assess safety and follow safeguarding procedures
live_plab_copy.why_correct: A disclosure of financial abuse with fear of a relative is a safeguarding concern for an adult at risk, so the clinician should take it seriously, assess immediate safety and follow local adult safeguarding procedures (Care Act 2014).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Raising it with the alleged abuser in front of the patient could escalate risk. B. Practical advice alone leaves a vulnerable adult at risk and does not meet safeguarding duties. C. Documentation without action leaves a vulnerable adult at risk. E. Financial abuse is a recognised form of abuse under adult safeguarding, and clinicians have a duty to act.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Financial abuse is a recognised form of adult abuse; a disclosure, especially with fear of the relative, must be taken seriously, with immediate safety assessed and local adult safeguarding procedures followed.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Older adult frightened of a relative ↓ Discloses money being taken ↓ Financial abuse of an adult at risk ↓ Safeguarding duty applies ↓ Take seriously, assess safety and follow safeguarding procedures
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, discussing the allegation with the relative present — openness sounds fair, but confronting the alleged abuser in front of the patient may escalate the risk.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Disclosure of financial abuse is a safeguarding concern: assess safety and act.

live_plab_copy.stem: A doctor encounters a clinical problem outside their competence. What is the appropriate action?

options.A: Manage it using online guidance without involving others
options.B: Advise the patient to arrange their own private specialist
options.C: Defer all decisions until the next outpatient clinic
options.D: Seek advice or refer to a colleague with the expertise
options.E: Proceed after reading about the condition overnight

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Seek advice or refer to a colleague with the expertise
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Doctors should recognise the limits of their competence and seek appropriate assistance.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Acting outside competence on the basis of online guidance alone is unsafe. B. The doctor should arrange appropriate help rather than leave the patient to find it. C. Unnecessary delay may harm the patient. E. Reading about a condition does not confer competence to manage it.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Recognising and working within the limits of your competence is a core professional duty; seek senior or specialist advice or refer, so that the patient is neither harmed nor delayed.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, Proceed after reading overnight — self-study looks conscientious, but reading does not confer competence and still delays proper help.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Outside your competence: seek help or refer rather than improvise.

A newly qualified doctor assesses a deteriorating patient but is unsure how to manage the situation safely.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Continue managing alone to build confidence and competence
options.B: Wait to discuss the patient at the next ward round
options.C: Seek senior help early while continuing immediate care
options.D: Ask a fellow foundation doctor for advice and avoid escalating
options.E: Document concerns and review again in four hours

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Seek senior help early while continuing immediate care

live_plab_copy.pearl: Recognising the limits of your competence is a professional duty: with a deteriorating patient you are unsure how to manage, call senior help early while continuing immediate ABCDE care.
live_plab_copy.thinking: The GMC expects doctors to recognise the limits of their competence, seek advice when appropriate and provide safe care.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, asking a fellow foundation doctor — it feels less exposing than escalating, but an equally inexperienced colleague does not replace senior input for a deteriorating patient.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Unsure with a deteriorating patient: call for senior help early and keep treating.

A patient with long-standing Crohn disease develops recurrent crampy abdominal pain, vomiting and abdominal distension.

Which complication could explain these symptoms?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Chronic transmural inflammation and fibrosis in Crohn disease can produce strictures and obstructive symptoms.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids cause rectal bleeding or pain and do not cause obstructive symptoms. C. Gastro-oesophageal reflux causes heartburn, not crampy pain with vomiting and distension. D. An anal fissure causes painful defecation and does not cause bowel obstruction. E. Acute hepatitis causes jaundice and malaise rather than crampy pain, vomiting and distension.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Crohn disease is transmural, so chronic inflammation and fibrosis can narrow the bowel, commonly the terminal ileum, causing obstructive episodes.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Long-standing Crohn disease ↓ Transmural inflammation and fibrosis ↓ Crampy pain, vomiting, distension ↓ Obstructive picture ↓ Stricture causing bowel obstruction
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, severe gastro-oesophageal reflux disease — vomiting may suggest an upper GI cause, but reflux causes heartburn, not crampy pain with distension.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Obstructive symptoms in Crohn disease: think stricture.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Colitis with systemic toxicity and a dilated colon means toxic megacolon.

live_plab_copy.pearl: Diverticulosis means diverticula without symptoms, diverticular disease means diverticula causing symptoms, and diverticulitis means inflamed or infected diverticula.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Sigmoid diverticula on CT ↓ Recurrent pain, constipation and distension ↓ Symptomatic, with no infection described ↓ Diverticular disease
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, colonic Crohn disease — another cause of recurrent abdominal pain, but it causes patchy transmural inflammation, not sigmoid diverticula on CT.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Symptomatic diverticula without inflammation = diverticular disease.

Patchy transmural inflammation is characteristic of Crohn disease, not IBS. E. Mucosal ulceration and bleeding suggest another diagnosis.
live_plab_copy.pearl: IBS is a disorder of gut–brain interaction: symptoms are real, but there is no inflammation, ulceration or raised cancer risk, which is reassuring to explain.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Patient with IBS ↓ Worried about bowel damage ↓ IBS has no structural or inflammatory pathology ↓ Functional disorder without structural damage
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, mucosal changes raising cancer risk — a common fear, but IBS does not increase colorectal cancer risk; that concern applies to long-standing colitis.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: IBS is functional: real symptoms without structural damage or cancer risk.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, pernicious anaemia — autoimmune gastritis can impair iron absorption, but it is not the priority; occult GI cancer must be excluded first.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency in an older adult means investigate for GI cancer.
